To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the long-term effects of civil conflict are negative for democracy, and that these effects operate through the following mechanisms: 1) conflict weakens political institutions; 2) it increases elite factionalism and reduces elite cohesion; 3) it leads to a militarisation of politics and the creation of a'military state' which is hostile to democracy; 4) it increases the risk of state collapse and the return to conflict.

war has had a negative effect on the quality of political parties and institutions, the degree to which political elites are able to work together, and the extent to which civil military relations are democratic.

(i) in the three high conflict cases, the legacy of conflict has undermined the quality of political and military institutions, (ii) the legacy of conflict undermined elite cohesion and, (iii) in the three cases where conflict was most intense and protracted, the legacy of war undermined the nature of civil-military relations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how war shapes the process of democratic consolidation.
how war and violence shape the nature of the state and the prospects for democratisation.
the relationship between war and democracy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a negative relationship between war and democratic consolidation in East Africa, but that this is not a simple relationship, and is contingent on a range of other factors.
the legacy of conflict on democracy is negative, but not always and in all cases.
there is little evidence to support the view that war promotes democracy in Africa.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

(i) the quality of political and civil institutions is the most important factor in explaining differences in democratisation outcomes; (ii) civil war is likely to lead to a breakdown of elite cohesion and to a weakening of the state, and (iii) civil war can lead to a militarisation of the political sphere, with negative implications for democratisation.
war is not a good thing, and that the legacy of conflict can be very long indeed.
war undermines democracy in Africa.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the impact of war on democracy is likely to be mediated by factors such as the nature of the state, the nature of the conflict, the nature of external intervention, the nature of elite cohesion, the nature of civil society and the nature of the international environment.
the relationship between war and democracy is complex.
the impact of violent conflict on the quality of democratic institutions in Africa is not uniform.
